conditions.post_mortem_regions: firmware shared pages and six job firmware objects 0x41c00000 (51 pages), job payload 0x41090000 (88 pages), GPU page tables 0x410e8000 (32 pages), read with sunxi-fel after the return to FEL

conclusion: The job faulted on its first load because the PDS pointer constants were stored high word first. The firmware reset the compute context (event 105, reason GUILTY_LOCKUP, page fault at GPU address 0x80), ran the UPDATE after it (timeline 1) and left the output untouched. The image refused the context-reset event, failed its control, did not send the cleanup, and the stop refused to start, leaving the GPU powered with the firmware running. Fixed by storing the constants low word first (pvr_compute_job.c doutw_pair, in the single-dispatch, grid and multi-dispatch forms; the tile pair keeps the first index in the low half; the context store and load programs in pvr_compute_programs.c are stored low word first too).
narrative:
Log:
GPU FWJ job complete=0 outcome=4 stage=4 phase=4 error=0 client=7 client_error=0 kick_status=0x0 timeline=0x1
GPU FWJ output w0=0xd1a3566f w1=0x2f64cf9c w31=0xb88a0ade guard=0x6d35a7c1 expected0=0x2e5ca990 expected31=0x4775f521
GPU FWJ cleanup status=0xffffffff events=0 kccb_done=0x2 pow_state=0x3
FAIL GPU firmware stop refused, GPU left running
Stage 4: the job had started; phase 4 is PVR_JOB_KICK and client 7 is PVR_CCCB_WAIT (the KICK sent and waiting to be settled); outcome 4 is the transport: the control failed, not the timeline or the output. The firmware consumed the KICK (executed count 1 to 2), set the timeline to 1 (the job's UPDATE value) and raised its interrupt, which the image read and cleared (accesses 104 and 105). The output is the image's own fill, the complement of each expected word (0xd1a3566f XOR 0x2e5ca990 = 0xffffffff, likewise w1 and w31); guards intact; no GPU store reached those words. The progress record ends at access 105; the second interrupt read never came, so the control failed on a firmware event it refused, a restart request, or a KICK return word with bits beyond 0-2; the host model reproduces every logged line with each (check.py --fw-job --board-log). The cleanup was not sent (0xffffffff is the image's initial value) because the image sent it only after a complete job.
Likely causes listed before the post-mortem, most likely first: the USC program had never executed on hardware; no MMUCACHE before the first KICK (both references always send it); read-only bits on program, stream, input and border pages, which upstream never sets; CDM command flags 0x24 (prevent overlap, single core), which Mesa sets for barriers or atomics. A step-by-step comparison with upstream, the DDK and Mesa found the context, client CCB commands, KICK, page-table entry formats, CDM stream, cleanup and CPU cache maintenance matching. The lockup detector limit of the context is 30,000 ms, so the fault within about a millisecond was an MMU page fault or USC error.
Post-mortem decode (structures from pvr_rogue_fwif.h, pvr_rogue_fwif_check.h, pvr_rogue_cr_defs.h and the DDK rgxmhdefs_km.h): the firmware CCB held one command (write and read offset 1), 0x2abc0069 = 105, the context reset notification, with context 1, reason 1 (GUILTY_LOCKUP), data master 4 (CDM), job reference 1, flags 0x1 (page fault), page catalogue 0x410e8000 (the job's) and fault address 0x80. Recovery record (0x8000, rogue_fwif_hwrinfobuf): count 1; record 0 type 3 (BIF0FAULT), data master 4, recovery flags 0x20; CDM locked-up and recovered counts each 1. BIF request status 0x0010100000000080 with the XE memory hierarchy (core 36.0.104.183, feature word 0x000002181d51bf35, bit 41): bit 52 set, a read; tag ID 16, MCU_USCA, a USC data access; tag sideband 0; address bits 4-39 = 0x80. MMU status 0x1041: fault, data type 2, 4 KB pages, catalogue base 1; page catalogue 0x410e8000. System data: power state IDLE (3), HWR state flag 1. Kernel CCB write and read offsets 2 (health check and KICK consumed, no return words). The job's client CCB control (0x2f000): write, read and dependency offsets all 0xb8, wrap mask 0x3ff, so the firmware took both the CDM and UPDATE commands. Timeline 1.
Page tables were correct and the address was not: GPU address 0x80 falls in invalid catalogue entry 0. The input 0x8001140000 walks catalogue entry 512, directory entry 8, table entry 320 to 0x410a6000; the output 0x8001190000 walks to 0x410a7000 with the cache-bypass bit, as built. The job's PDS data at 0x410a3000 stored each pointer high word first: 0x80, 0x01140000 for the input and 0x80, 0x01190040 for the output. A DOUTW writes data word 0 to the even register and the program reads the low half from the even register, so the input pointer became 0x0114000000000080, whose 40-bit bus address is 0x80 (the fault address); the output pointer would have given 0x4000000080; the fault was the program's first load, of seed and factor. The DOUTU task word in the same segment is stored low word first and the USC did run. Mesa's end-of-tile and clear-colour DOUTWs put word 0 in the destination register (pvr_pds.c:570-573, 3238-3247); only its save-restore generator, whose layout the job's PDS reference followed, stores the high word first (pvr_pds.c:3664-3667), while Mesa's own store and load shaders read the low half from register 0 (usclib/common.cl:181, pvr_iface.h:117-122). The context store and load program constants (0xda, 0x00240000 and 0xda, 0x00290000) would fault near 0xd0; the fence and end programs have no DOUTW constants; the context resume stream is zero.
The payload and page tables were byte for byte what the set-27 image composed (replayed in the host model with no GPU write): the output page held the image's fill and no other byte of the 88 pages changed. In the shared pages only firmware-owned words differed: queue offsets, the recovery record, system and OS data counters, the client CCB offsets, one word of the context state and the VM record's catalogue-register field (0xffffffff to 0; the MMU status names catalogue base 1, which the decode does not explain). Trace buffers unchanged.
Image changes after the run: events 101-108 are recorded without failing the control; a consumed KICK is settled after the job so its pending slot cannot fail the kernel CCB; the cleanup is sent whenever the firmware has finished with the context; when the control failed or the firmware acknowledges neither power request, the stop runs without the acknowledgements as upstream's hard reset does (register sequence and, when every idle poll matches, the OFF); new log lines report the control error, events, a context reset's words, the client CCB read offset, the KICK return word, the MMU command status and the first recovery record. The reference byte checks (checks/pvr-compute-job.c, pvr-compute-package.c, pvr-compute-programs.c) pass Mesa's generator each value with its halves exchanged, and check.py --fw-job checks the job's constants in the linked image; the set-27 image fails that check.

A wrong output with intact guards would mean wrong inputs or state; an unchanged timeline with the KICK consumed would mean the firmware could not run the command; a context reset prints its reason and fault address; in each case the stop and OFF still run, with the firmware's acknowledgements or without them when the idle checks pass.

conclusion: Every prediction held. mmu_status=0x1 is the return word of the MMUCACHE command (ROGUE_FWIF_KCCB_RTN_SLOT_CMD_EXECUTED, pvr_rogue_fwif.h:1765), not a recovery field nor the catalogue-base field left open by the set-27 post-mortem; count=0 is the empty recovery record. The firmware wrote return word 1 for MMUCACHE and the cleanup (and rtn1=0x1 for the forced-idle request) but none for the health check or the KICK, which upstream also sends without waiting on a slot. Six kernel commands ran: health check, MMUCACHE, KICK, cleanup and the two power requests. The image logs no time for the job itself, so the KICK-to-timeline time is bounded only by the 25.75 ms remainder.

hypothesis: Host checks cover the first-job image, the client ring, the stop without acknowledgements and their cost.
narrative: Cost: one job per run adds three KCCB commands (MMUCACHE, the KICK and the cleanup), 88 page cleans, the table publication and a 200 ms bound to the firmware-stop image, inside the 1.5 s session with the monitor's 500 ms margin; the stop keeps its 300 ms, of which the stop without acknowledgements takes the last 100 ms. The image's log in the host check is at most 11,311 of 16,128 bytes. Checks: checks/pvr-cccb.py (the ring's reference bytes and the KICK consumed without a return word); apps/gpu-power-id/check.py --fw-job has thirteen cases on the linked image with a model of the firmware and GPU that runs the client CCB's CDM and UPDATE commands: the complete job, also with a KICK return word and with a statistics event; a timeline that never moves; a wrong word; a broken guard; a cleanup without a return word; a context-reset event with and without the output; set 27's signature (fj-board-1025); a restart request; a bad KICK return word; no acknowledgement of the power requests, with and without an idle GPU. With --board-log the set-27 image reproduces every logged line of set 27 under three of these models. Every case's start is the firmware-start sequence access for access, and every later GPU access is an interrupt read or clear, a kick and its read-back, or the next stop step. check.py --fw-stop passes ten cases, three new or changed. checks/pvr-gpu-stop.c (122 retained faults) and checks/pvr-gpu-stop-reference.py pass; the second compares the unacknowledged plan with upstream's pvr_fw_stop, final reset included. The job runs on the single-core profile that the A733 user manual documents (MC1); the image does not read the core-count registers 0xf308 and 0xf300 that the service's pvr_compute_mode admission reads.
